sections.Kurzabstract: The STARS-D is suitable for research purposes to assess students' anxiety with regard to statistics. It can also be used for counselling students, for example in the case of learning and study difficulties. It consists of 51 items with two superordinate scales (1 Anxiety about statistics, 2 Attitude towards statistics). Scale (1) comprises, with 23 items, the subscales (a) Anxiety in statistics classes and statistics exams, (b) Anxiety about interpreting statistical results and (c) Anxiety about asking for help. Scale (2) comprises, with 28 items, the subscales (d) academic self-concept in statistics, (e) Value of statistics and (f) Attitude towards statistics instructors. Reliability: The test-retest correlations, apart from that of the scale "Anxiety about asking for help", are in a satisfactory to very good range. The two total scales also show very good test-retest reliabilities. The internal consistencies lie between alpha = .80 and .99 (exception: subscale "Anxiety about asking for help"). Validity: A six-factor model as well as a six-factor model with two superordinate factors were demonstrated by factor analysis. In a laboratory experiment as well as in field studies, significant results could be obtained.
sections.Diagnostische Zielsetzung: The instrument is suitable for research purposes to assess the anxiety of students (tertiary education sector) with regard to statistics. It can also be used for counselling students, for example in the case of learning and study difficulties.
sections.Aufbau: The STARS-D questionnaire consists of a total of 51 items. They are divided into two superordinate scales that assess anxiety about and attitude towards statistics, respectively. The scale "Anxiety about statistics" comprises, with 23 items, the subscales: (a) Anxiety in statistics classes and statistics exams, (b) Anxiety about interpreting statistical results and (c) Anxiety about asking for help. When completing it, the test takers rate situations that have to do with statistics on a rating scale from 1 (no feeling of anxiety) to 5 (strong feeling of anxiety). The scale "Attitude towards statistics" comprises, with 28 items, the subscales: (d) academic self-concept in statistics, (e) Value of statistics, (f) Attitude towards statistics instructors. The items are rated on a scale from 1 (I absolutely disagree) to 5 (I absolutely agree). The questionnaire can be administered as a group test.
sections.Grundlagen und Konstruktion: The STARS-D questionnaire is based on the English-language STARS by Cruise, Cash and Bolton (1985), which is one of the most frequently used instruments for assessing statistics anxiety. It regards statistics anxiety as a multidimensional construct that comprises, on the one hand, the experience of anxiety in different statistics-related situations and, on the other hand, the attitude towards statistics. The instrument has so far been used predominantly for research purposes to assess students' anxiety with regard to statistics. The studies on statistics anxiety show associations between statistics anxiety and behaviour that impedes learning, such as procrastination. However, anxiety about statistics can have different effects. Statistics anxiety can promote state anxiety in the exam and thus negatively influence performance. In certain situations, anxiety can also have an activating effect on learning and preparing for an exam, e.g. when the consequences of failing the exam are perceived as more serious than the anxiety about the subject.
sections.Empirische Prüfung und Gütekriterien:
Reliability: The test-retest correlations, apart from that of the scale "Anxiety about asking for help", are in a satisfactory to very good range. The two total scales also show very good test-retest reliabilities. The internal consistencies of the subscales, like the internal consistencies of the two total scales, are in a very good range, with values between alpha = .80 and alpha = .99. Only the value for the subscale "Anxiety about asking for help" is lower.
Validity: Various structural models were examined by means of confirmatory factor analysis with a robust maximum likelihood estimator (Muthen & Muthen, 2009). The examination yielded two equivalent structural models that could explain the data equally well. In the first model, the items could be assigned to six factors: (a) Anxiety in statistics classes and statistics exams, (b) Anxiety about interpreting statistical results, (c) Anxiety about asking for help, (d) academic self-concept in statistics, (e) Value of statistics and (f) Attitude towards statistics instructors. A structure with six plus two superordinate factors, (1) Anxiety about statistics and (2) Attitude towards statistics, proved to be equivalent to this model. In model 2, the subfactors (a), (b) and (c) are subordinate to factor (1), and the subfactors (d), (e) and (f) to factor 2. In a laboratory experiment, associations were examined between the two global scales Anxiety about and Attitude towards statistics, trait anxiety, the subjective assessment of tension and state anxiety in the current experiment, and physiological parameters. The attitude towards statistics correlated significantly with a cardiovascular response pattern during the experimental statistics exam situation that is characteristic of aversive situations in which persons feel unable to cope with the situation actively and therefore tend towards passive coping strategies such as avoidance. Significant associations also emerged between anxiety about statistics and self-rated state anxiety in the exam situation. Further evidence for validity emerged in field studies. The scale "Anxiety about statistics" was able to predict subjectively rated state anxiety in an actual statistics exam.
Norms: Only means and standard deviations from samples for various scientific studies are available.
sections.Testkonzept/Theoretischer Hintergrund:
Statistics anxiety describes those feelings of anxiety and discomfort that persons experience when they are confronted with statistical content or tasks or when they are in a learning situation that has to do with statistics (e.g. attending a statistics course or taking a statistics exam). Statistics anxiety is regarded as an enduring personality trait, i.e. a person with statistics anxiety always experiences more anxiety in statistics-related situations than a person without statistics anxiety.
When students are asked in which courses they feel particularly high anxiety, a high proportion name courses in statistics. This applies especially to fields of study such as educational science, psychology or social-science fields of study, which are chosen by persons with less interest and a more negative academic self-concept with regard to mathematics and natural sciences (Onwuegbuzie, 2004; Ruggeri et al., 2008; Macher, Paechter, Papousek, & Ruggeri, 2012). Statistics anxiety can hinder students in their academic progress, e.g. when students with statistics anxiety achieve poorer exam results, postpone exams or drop out of courses and even theses.
Statistics anxiety is a specific form of anxiety that occurs in specific situations. Empirical studies show that it correlates partly with trait anxiety, but that a substantial proportion of statistics anxiety cannot be explained by trait anxiety, so that statistics anxiety represents a genuine form of anxiety (Macher et al., 2012).
The STARS-D questionnaire (Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale - deutsche Fassung) is based on the English-language questionnaire by Cruise, Cash and Bolton (1985), which is one of the most frequently used instruments for assessing statistics anxiety. It regards statistics anxiety as a multidimensional construct that comprises, on the one hand, the experience of anxiety in different statistics-related situations and, on the other hand, students' attitude towards statistics.
The instrument has so far been used predominantly for research purposes to investigate the influence of statistics anxiety on learning, exam preparation and exam performance (Macher et al., 2012; Macher et al., 2013). The studies show associations between statistics anxiety and behaviour that impedes learning, such as procrastination. However, anxiety in statistics can have different effects. Thus, statistics anxiety can promote state anxiety in the exam and thus negatively influence performance. In certain situations, however, anxiety can also have an activating effect on learning and preparing for an exam, e.g. when the consequences of failing the exam are perceived as more serious than the anxiety about the subject (Macher et al., 2012; Pekrun, 1988).
The STARS-D questionnaire is suitable both for research purposes and for counselling students, e.g. in the case of learning and study difficulties. It is the only instrument for assessing statistics anxiety that is available in German.
sections.Testkonzept/Testaufbau:
The STARS-D questionnaire consists of a total of 51 items. They are divided into two superordinate scales that assess anxiety about and attitude towards statistics, respectively. The two superordinate scales each comprise three subscales.
The total scale "Anxiety about statistics" comprises the subscales: (a) Anxiety in statistics classes and statistics exams (8 items), (b) Anxiety about interpreting statistical results (11 items) and (c) Anxiety about asking for help (4 items). These 23 items describe situations that have to do with statistics. When completing it, persons rate on a rating scale from 1 (no feeling of anxiety) to 5 (strong feeling of anxiety) how much anxiety they would experience in the respective situation.
The total scale "Attitude towards statistics" comprises the subscales: (d) academic self-concept in statistics (7 items), (e) Value of statistics (15 items) and (f) Attitude towards statistics instructors (6 items). The 28 items describe attitudes and statements about statistics that are rated on a scale from 1 (I absolutely disagree) to 5 (I absolutely agree).
sections.Testkonzept/Auswertungshilfen: No templates, scoring programs or interpretation aids such as cut-off values, norms, confidence limits or critical differences are available. Templates can, however, easily be made oneself.
sections.Testkonzept/Auswertungszeit: If the questionnaire is scored by hand, approx. 15 minutes per case should be expected. It is recommended to score the data with software support.
sections.Durchführung/Testformen: The STARS-D questionnaire can be administered as a group or individual test. It is based on the English-language questionnaire of the same name by Cruise et al. (1985).
sections.Durchführung/Altersbereiche: The questionnaire is suitable for use with students from approximately 18 years of age.
sections.Durchführung/Durchführungszeit: The time for completion is approx. 15 minutes. The test takers are given no time limit for completing it.
sections.Durchführung/Material: The questionnaire is presented as a paper-pencil test. Beyond this, only a pen is needed to answer the questions.
sections.Durchführung/Instruktion: The instructions are standardised and printed on the questionnaire; they do not have to be read aloud.
sections.Durchführung/Durchführungsvoraussetzunge: No special qualifications are required to administer the instrument.
sections.Testkonstruktion:
The English-language STARS questionnaire was developed by Cruise et al. (1985) and is to this day the most frequently used instrument for assessing anxiety about statistics and attitudes towards statistics. The development of the English-language version began with 89 items, which were checked by experts with regard to their face validity. In a series of factor analyses, a structure with 51 items could be identified that could be assigned to six factors (Cruise et al., 1985). Of these, three assess statistics anxiety in the narrower sense and three the attitudes towards statistics.
For the English-language version, various validation studies based on classical test theory are available with samples of students from the USA, England and South Africa (Baloglu, 2003; Cruise et al., 1985; Hanna, Shevlin & Dempster, 2008; Keeley, Zayac & Correia, 2008; Mji & Onwuegbuzie, 2004; Watson et al., 2003). In the studies, internal consistency coefficients between alpha = .64 and alpha = .94 emerged for the six factors. In two administrations four weeks apart, Cruise et al. (1985) found test-retest reliabilities between rtt = .67 and rtt = .83 (n = 121). In a study by Keeley et al. (2008), test-retest reliabilities between rtt = .76 and rtt = .87 emerged with a two-week interval between the measurements and rtt = .41 to rtt = .74 with a four-month interval (n = 83). In examining the factorial structure of the English version, Hanna et al. (2008) argued for a model with six individual factors. However, they did not examine the possibility of a model with two superordinate factors, statistics anxiety in the narrower sense and attitudes towards statistics, although both the items and the response formats would suggest such a model.
The validity of the English-language questionnaire has so far been assessed only by examining the internal structure and the correlation with other assessment instruments for statistics anxiety (Cruise et al., 1985; Hanna et al., 2008; Mji & Onwuegbuzie, 2004). An examination of the criterion-related validity of the English-language questionnaire is still pending.
The construction of the German-language version STARS-D was based on the 51 items of the English-language version. In a first step, the factorial structure was examined by means of confirmatory factor analysis in a sample of 400 students of psychology and educational science. Two structural models proved to be equivalent, a structure with six factors and a structure with six plus two superordinate factors (statistics anxiety, attitude towards statistics; Papousek et al., 2012). Validity was examined in a laboratory experiment and in the field. Among other things, associations emerged between the scale statistics anxiety and the perception of state anxiety in a statistics exam situation created in the laboratory, as well as between the attitude towards statistics and physiological parameters indicating certain coping strategies (Papousek et al., 2012).
sections.Gütekriterien/Objektivität: Owing to the standardised instruction, the STARS-D questionnaire can be assessed as objective with regard to its administration.

sections.Gütekriterien/Validität:
Structure of the questionnaire:
The factorial structure was examined in a sample of 400 students of the Karl-Franzens-Universität Graz who were attending an introductory course in statistics (317 women and 83 men between 18 and 46 years old, M = 21.2, SD = 3.9). 293 students were enrolled in psychology and 107 in educational science. The distribution of men and women in the sample corresponds to the distribution in the two fields of study. The data were collected in several courses taught by two different lecturers. Various structural models were examined by means of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with a robust maximum likelihood estimator (Mplus 5.21, Muthen & Muthen, 2009). The examination yielded two equivalent structural models, both of which could explain the data equally well.
In the first model, the items could be assigned to six factors: (a) Anxiety in statistics classes and statistics exams, (b) Anxiety about interpreting statistical results, (c) Anxiety about asking for help, (d) academic self-concept in statistics, (e) Value of statistics and (f) Attitude towards statistics instructors. The CFA showed acceptable fit indices (RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .07, CFI = .91; Papousek et al., 2012). A structure with two superordinate factors, (1) "Anxiety about statistics" and (2) "Attitude towards statistics" (RMSEA = .06, SRMR = .05, CFI = .91), proved to be equivalent to this model. In model 2, the subfactors (a), (b) and (c) are subordinate to factor (1), and the subfactors (d), (e) and (f) to factor 2.
Association of statistics anxiety and attitude towards statistics, respectively, with physiological parameters and state anxiety in a laboratory experiment:
In a laboratory experiment, associations were examined between the two superordinate scales (Anxiety about statistics, Attitude towards statistics), trait anxiety, the subjective assessment of tension and state anxiety in the current experiment, and physiological parameters such as heart rate and blood pressure. 66 first-semester psychology students (49 women and 17 men between 18 and 43 years old, M = 21.0, SD = 4.2) completed the questionnaires STARS-D and STAI-T (assessment of trait anxiety) one month to several months before the laboratory experiment. In the laboratory experiment, they were instructed to answer a question on statistics that corresponds to the subject-matter standard of the statistics exam. The answer would be recorded and subsequently evaluated.
The previously assessed attitude towards statistics (total scale) correlated significantly with the cardiovascular response pattern during the experimental statistics exam situation (r = .34). Persons with a negative attitude towards statistics predominantly showed vascular reactions that are typical when persons perceive a situation as aversive, feel overwhelmed and feel unable to cope with the situation actively (Gramer, 2003). The scale "Anxiety about statistics" also correlated positively with self-rated state anxiety in the exam situation (r = .42).
Association of statistics anxiety and attitude towards statistics with state anxiety in the exam:
96 first-semester psychology students completed the questionnaires STARS-D and STAI-T (assessment of trait anxiety) one week before their statistics exam. At the time of the exam, immediately before the exam papers were handed out, they completed two items of the Kurz-Skala Stimmung/Aktivierung (KUSTA; Binz & Wendt, 1986), with which they rated their current anxiety and tension (Papousek et al., 2012). In a hierarchical regression, state anxiety (KUSTA) was used as the criterion. In the first step, trait anxiety was entered into the regression equation as a predictor, then the two STARS-D total scales were included in the regression simultaneously. Of the two superordinate scales, only anxiety about statistics contributes significantly to the prediction of state anxiety (beta = .48). Also in the prediction of tension at the time of the exam, only the statistics anxiety total scale showed a significant contribution (beta = .37). These results speak for the criterion validity of the STARS-D questionnaire.
sections.Gütekriterien/Normierung: No norms are available. Means and standard deviations from samples for various scientific studies can be looked up in Macher et al. (2012), Macher et al. (2013) and Papousek et al. (2012).
sections.Anwendungsmöglichkeiten: The STARS-D questionnaire is used in particular in the research context. In addition, the instrument is also suitable for counselling students with learning difficulties in statistics.
sections.Bewertung: The STARS-D questionnaire is an economical instrument for the self-report of anxiety about statistics and attitude towards statistics. The questionnaire is characterised by simple and quick administration and scoring. The assumed structure of the questionnaire and of the concept of anxiety about and attitude towards statistics could be confirmed in a validation study. The test-retest reliabilities are in the satisfactory to very good range. For validity, various pieces of evidence were collected in laboratory and field studies. The questionnaire is suitable for scientific purposes but can also be used in counselling students.

The previously assessed attitude towards statistics (total scale) correlated significantly with the cardiovascular response pattern during the experimental statistics exam situation (r = .34). Persons with a negative attitude towards statistics predominantly showed vascular reactions that are typical when persons perceive a situation as aversive, feel overwhelmed and feel unable to cope with the situation actively (Gramer, 2003). The scale "Anxiety about statistics" also correlated positively with self-rated state anxiety in the exam situation (r = .42).
Association of statistics anxiety and attitude towards statistics with state anxiety in the exam:
96 first-semester psychology students completed the questionnaires STARS-D and STAI-T (assessment of trait anxiety) one week before their statistics exam. At the time of the exam, immediately before the exam papers were handed out, they completed two items of the Kurz-Skala Stimmung/Aktivierung (KUSTA; Binz & Wendt, 1986), with which they rated their current anxiety and tension (Papousek et al., 2012). In a hierarchical regression, state anxiety (KUSTA) was used as the criterion. In the first step, trait anxiety was entered into the regression equation as a predictor, then the two STARS-D total scales were included in the regression simultaneously. Of the two superordinate scales, only anxiety about statistics contributes significantly to the prediction of state anxiety (beta = .48). Also in the prediction of tension at the time of the exam, only the statistics anxiety total scale showed a significant contribution (beta = .37). These results speak for the criterion validity of the STARS-D questionnaire.
Study.Norming: No norms are available. Means and standard deviations from samples for various scientific studies can be looked up in Macher et al. (2012), Macher et al. (2013) and Papousek et al. (2012).
